Boris Yeltsin (1 February 1931 - 23 April 2007) was a Soviet and Russian politician who served as President of Russia from 1991 to 1999.

Charon (-n; Ancient) is the ferryman of the Greek underworld.

Before becoming UK Prime Minister in 2007, this Labour politician spent a decade as Chancellor of the Exchequer under Tony Blair — who is he?
Gordon Brown (born 20 February 1951) is a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Leader of the Labour Party from 2007 to 2010.

Historians often treat this ancient Semitic-speaking people as equivalent to another biblical group, with the name traditionally applied to their nomadic era before a kingdom arose in the 11th century BCE — who were they?

House of Saud is the ruling royal family of Saudi Arabia.

A former Carlyle Group partner and investment banker, this attorney served as the 16th chair of the Federal Reserve from 2018 to 2026 — who is he?
Jerome Powell (born February 4, 1953) is an American central banker and attorney who served as the 16th chair of the Federal Reserve from 2018 to 2026.
Whose son Bernardo became President of Guatemala in 2024, decades after this philosophy-professor-turned-statesman first won the office democratically in 1945?
Juan José Arévalo (10 September 1904 - 8 October 1990) was a Guatemalan statesman and professor of philosophy who became Guatemala's first democratically elected president in 1945.

Maximilien Robespierre (6 May 1758 - 28 July 1794) was a French lawyer and statesman, widely recognised as one of the most influential figures of the French Revolution.

Rafic Hariri (1 November 1944 - 14 February 2005) was a Lebanese businessman and politician who served as prime minister of Lebanon from 1992 to 1998 and again from 2000 to 2004.
A human-rights lawyer who rode a wave of younger internet users into office, he became South Korea's ninth president in 2003 — which leader of the so-called '386 Generation' was it?
Roh Moo-hyun (1 September 1946 - 23 May 2009) was a South Korean politician and lawyer who served as the ninth president of South Korea from 2003 to 2008.

A renowned scholar of comparative religion who held endowed chairs at Calcutta and Oxford, he climbed from ambassador to the Soviet Union all the way to the presidency of India — who was this philosopher-statesman?

In Norse mythology, these female figures choose which slain warriors are worthy to be guided to Odin's hall, where they serve the fallen mead between preparations for Ragnarök — what are they called?

Lebanese Civil War: 1975–1990 conflict in Lebanon. The Lebanese Civil War (Arabic: الحرب الأهلية اللبنانية, al-ḥarb al-ahliyyah al-libnāniyyah) was a multifaceted armed conflict that took place from 1975 to 1990.

In what year did B. R. Ambedkar die?

Semen: prostate. Semen, also known as seminal fluid, is a bodily fluid that contains spermatozoa from the male gonads of animals.
Who is credited with discovering Niobium?
Niobium: Charles Hatchett. Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb (formerly columbium, Cb) and atomic number 41.
Who is credited with discovering Peroxisome?
Peroxisome: Christian de Duve. A peroxisome is a membrane-bound organelle, a type of microbody, found in the cytoplasm of virtually all eukaryotic cells.
Who is credited with discovering Uncertainty principle?
Uncertainty principle: Werner Heisenberg. The uncertainty principle, also known as Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics.
Who is credited with discovering Mensa?
Mensa (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for table, though it originally commemorated Table Mountain and was known as "Mons Mensae".

The first woman to officially attend a Dutch university, she became one of the Netherlands' earliest female physicians and, in 1882, opened the world's first birth control clinic — who was this suffrage leader?
Aletta Jacobs (Dutch; 9 February 1854 - 10 August 1929) was a Dutch physician and women's suffrage activist.
Multicellular, oxygen-breathing, and all descended from a single common ancestor, this kingdom ranges in size from 8.5 micrometers to 33.6 meters. What is it?
Animal are multicellular, eukaryotic organisms belonging to the biological kingdom Animalia.

This German philosopher's 1818 masterwork describes the visible world as the manifestation of a blind, irrational underlying will, building on Kantian idealism while rejecting German idealism's optimism — who is he?
Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 - 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.
Facing a shortage of staff, this American lawyer volunteered himself as chief prosecutor at the Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg and later championed an International Criminal Court — who was he?
Ben Ferencz (March 11, 1920 - April 7, 2023) was an American lawyer.
Belonging to the Colubridae family of venomous snakes and found only in Sub-Saharan Africa, this reptile's scientific name is Dispholidus typus — what is it commonly called?
Boomslang (or; Dispholidus typus) is a highly venomous snake in the family Colubridae.

Native to tropical Africa, this vine's fruit can be eaten young as a vegetable, or left to mature, dry out, and be hollowed into a ladle, bowl, drinking vessel, or musical instrument — name this plant?

Calabash (Lagenaria siceraria), also known as bottle gourd, white-flowered gourd, long melon, birdhouse gourd, New Guinea bean, New Guinea butter bean, Tasmania bean, zucca melon and opo squash, is a vine which is grown for its fruit.
Separated from the small intestine by the ileocecal valve, this pouch — whose Latin root means 'blind' — kicks off the large intestine and, in herbivores, helps ferment cellulose. What is it?
Cecum (plural ceca or) is a pouch within the peritoneum that is considered to be the beginning of the large intestine.

An organic compound found naturally in citrus fruits with the formula C6H8O7, over two million tons are manufactured annually for use as an acidifier, flavoring, and preservative. What is this compound?
Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7. In biochemistry, it is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, which occurs in the metabolism of all aerobic organisms.

What zoological term describes the internal-fertilization mating behavior in which a male animal introduces sperm directly into a female's reproductive tract — occurring via a 'cloacal kiss' in birds and most reptiles, or vaginally in mammals?
Copulation (zoology) is animal sexual behavior in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body, especially directly into the female's reproductive tract.
What unit of time, roughly 24 hours long, marks one full rotation of the Earth relative to the Sun and drives the circadian rhythms of most living things?
Day is the time period of a full rotation of the Earth with respect to the Sun.
This C-shaped first section of the small intestine connects the stomach to the jejunum and is the body's principal site for absorbing iron — what is it?
Duodenum is the first section of the small intestine in most vertebrates, including mammals, reptiles, and birds.
Built from flattened cells atop a columnar basal layer, this outer skin barrier regulates water loss and grows thinner as a person ages — what is it?
Epidermis is the outermost of the three major layers that constitute the skin, the inner layers being the dermis and hypodermis.

Named for a physicist who reportedly asked 'But where is everybody?' over lunch in 1950, this puzzle contrasts the vast odds of alien civilizations with our total lack of evidence for them — what's it called?
Fermi paradox is the term for the apparent gap between the lack of conclusive evidence of extraterrestrial civilizations and the apparently high likelihood of their existence.
Caused by a loss of blood supply, this type of tissue death most commonly affects the feet and hands and can turn skin red or black. What condition is it?
Gangrene is a type of tissue death caused by a lack of blood supply. If the gangrene is caused by an infectious agent, it may present with a fever or sepsis.
Defined as one joule of absorbed radiation energy per kilogram of matter, this SI measure is used in radiotherapy dosing and predicting acute radiation sickness — which measure is this?
Gray (unit) (symbol: Gy) is the unit of ionizing radiation dose in the International System of Units (SI), defined as the absorption of one joule of radiation energy per kilogram of matter.
Classified as acute if it resolves within six months and chronic if it persists longer, this inflammation of the liver can progress to cirrhosis or liver cancer — which condition?
Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver tissue. Acute hepatitis can resolve on its own, progress to chronic hepatitis, or (rarely) result in acute liver failure.

This altered mental state involves intensely focused attention, reduced awareness of surroundings, and heightened responsiveness to suggestion, though scientists still debate whether it's truly a distinct state of consciousness — what is it?

Hypnosis is a human condition involving focused attention (the selective attention/selective inattention hypothesis, SASI), reduced peripheral awareness, and an enhanced capacity to respond to suggestion.
Eaten raw or turned into jams and wine, this round Brazilian fruit is famous for growing directly on the trunk of its own tree — what is it?
Jabuticaba is a round, edible fruit produced by a jaboticaba tree (Plinia cauliflora), also known as Brazilian grapetree.
This Columbia economist won the Nobel in 2001 and famously skewers his laissez-faire colleagues as "free-market fundamentalists" — who is he?
Joseph Stiglitz (born February 9, 1943) is an American New Keynesian economist, a public policy analyst, political activist, and a professor at Columbia University.
What reddish-brown, alcohol-based tincture of opium, roughly 10% opium by weight, was historically sold without a prescription as a pain reliever and cough suppressant until the early 20th century?
Laudanum is a tincture of opium containing approximately 10% powdered opium by weight (the equivalent of 1% morphine).
Because its large profile and low operating altitude make it an easy target, this heavily armed gunship variant of the C-130 Hercules usually flies missions at night. What aircraft is it?
Lockheed AC-130 is a heavily armed, long-endurance, ground-attack variant of the C-130 Hercules transport, fixed-wing aircraft.

One of the most colorful mammals alive, this west-central African monkey wears red and blue on both its face and its rump, with the brightest males being the biggest — long mistaken for a baboon, what is it?
Mandrill (Mandrillus sphinx) is a large Old World monkey native to west central Africa.

Sold in Europe as part of a blended sedative called Mandrax alongside an antihistamine, this sedative-hypnotic drug of the quinazolinone class was pulled from many markets in the 1980s due to widespread misuse — name this compound?
Methaqualone is a sedative-hypnotic medication that was widely prescribed during the mid-20th century.

Sharing the insect order Lepidoptera with butterflies but typically sporting duller, darker wing patterns, this group includes roughly 160,000 mostly nocturnal species, many still undescribed by science — name this group of insects?
Moth are a group of winged insect of the order Lepidoptera, the other well-known members of which are butterflies, they are characterized by dark or dull patterned wings.
Found in tobacco and trace amounts of tomatoes and eggplants, this nightshade alkaloid is used recreationally as a stimulant yet acts as a deadly neurotoxin to insects — what is it?
Nicotine is an alkaloid found primarily in plants of the nightshade family, notably in tobacco; it is also synthesized.

Sitting in life's hierarchy between tissue and a full body system, this term describes a group of different tissues — like the epithelial and muscle layers of the gut wall — joined to serve one shared function. What is it?
Organ (biology) is a collection of tissues joined in a structural unit to serve a common function.

The males of this Phasianidae bird are famed for piercing calls and extravagant plumage; its Asiatic species include blue, green, and a third found only in the Congo Basin — what is this bird, collectively?

Peafowl is a common name for two bird species of the genus Pavo and one species of the closely related genus Afropavo within the tribe Pavonini of the family Phasianidae (the pheasants and their allies).

Enclosed in a papery husk formed from its calyx, the fruit of this nightshade-family genus tastes like a firm tomato crossed with a sweet, tangy grape — nearly half of its species grow only in Mexico. Name the genus?
Physalis (from Ancient) is a genus of approximately 75 to 90 flowering plants in the nightshade family (Solanaceae), which are native to the Americas and Australasia.
Element number 19, this silvery alkali metal reacts so eagerly with air that it forms flaky white peroxide within seconds — and its symbol K comes from the Neo-Latin word kalium. What is it?
Potassium is a chemical element; it has symbol K (from Neo-Latin kalium) and atomic number 19.
This collective name covers several genera of mid-sized game birds, split between Old World and New World families despite their similar appearance — what birds are they?
Quail is a collective name for several genera of mid-sized birds generally placed in the order Galliformes.

Winner of the 1905 Nobel Prize for his work on tuberculosis, this German physician identified the causative agents of tuberculosis, cholera, and anthrax, earning him the nickname 'father of microbiology' alongside Louis Pasteur — name this scientist?
Robert Koch (KOKH; 11 December 1843 - 27 May 1910) was a German physician and microbiologist.
This group of autoimmune diseases causes patches of thickened skin and poor blood flow to the fingers in cold weather, with one severe subtype called CREST syndrome — what condition is it?
Scleroderma is a group of autoimmune diseases that may result in changes to the skin, blood vessels, muscles, and internal organs.
This structural framework supporting an animal's body comes in three main forms — a rigid outer shell, a rigid inner frame, or a flexible fluid-supported structure — what is it called?
Skeleton is the structural frame that supports the body of most animals.

Described as the most extreme form of malnutrition, this severe shortfall of caloric energy is so grave that deliberately inflicting it on a population is a crime under international law — what is it?
Starvation is a severe deficiency in caloric energy intake, below the level needed to maintain an organism's life.

Restricted today to Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines, these tree-dwelling primates make up the only living family in their taxonomic order and thrive in liana-rich forests — which animal?
Tarsier are haplorhine primates of the family Tarsiidae, which is the lone extant family within the infraorder Tarsiiformes.
Found in nature only as an oxide and locked in minerals like rutile and ilmenite, this strong, silvery element bears the name of mythological giants — what is it?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
Native to cool climates across the Northern Hemisphere, this low shrub bears small, round, edible fruit of a deep blue color, and goes by several folk names depending on region — what's the species?
Vaccinium myrtillus is a holarctic species of shrub with edible fruit of blue color, known by the common names bilberry, blaeberry, and whortleberry.
This American child prodigy, son of a prominent psychiatrist, lectured on four-dimensional geometry at age 12 and graduated from Harvard cum laude at 16. Who was he?

William James Sidis (April 1, 1898 - July 17, 1944) was an American child prodigy whose exceptional abilities in mathematics and languages made him one of the most famous intellectual prodigies of the early 20th century.
A legendary Heian-era court diviner and astrologer, this figure lived 84 years free of illness, fueling belief in mystical powers — a Kyoto shrine bears his name today. Who is he?
A shortened-fuselage version of a popular narrow-body jetliner family, this aircraft entered service with Swissair in April 1996 and carries up to 156 passengers — which model?
Airbus A319: Airliner, shortened variant of the A320 family.

The brightest star in the constellation Aquila and a vertex of the Summer Triangle, this nearby A-type star spins so fast — about 286 km/s at its equator — that it bulges noticeably. Which star is it?
Altair: Brightest star in the constellation Aquila. Altair is the brightest star in the equatorial constellation of Aquila and the twelfth-brightest star in the night sky.

Affecting about 1 in 15,000 people, this rare genetic disorder causes severe intellectual disability, little to no speech, and balance problems — yet those affected are often noted for a notably happy personality. Which condition is it?
Angelman syndrome: Genetic disorder caused by a mutation of chromosome 15.
Nicknamed the strawberry tree for its red berries, this evergreen Mediterranean shrub is the national tree of Italy — which plant?
Arbutus unedo: Species of flowering plant in the heather family.
Affecting roughly one in five people at some point and usually starting in childhood, this long-term itchy, red, cracked-skin condition is also simply called eczema — what's its formal name?
Atopic dermatitis: Long-term form of skin inflammation.
A blood-feeding parasite of the genus Cimex that usually bites at night, this insect leaves itchy welts but, reassuringly, isn't known to spread any infectious disease — what is it?
Bed bug: Type of insect that feeds on human blood.

Also nicknamed 'buffalo gnats' or 'turkey gnats,' these small biting insects in the family Simuliidae feed mainly on nectar, though females also drink blood from birds and mammals — what are they called?
Black fly: Family of insects. Black flies or blackflies (sometimes called buffalo gnats, turkey gnats, or white socks) are flies in the family Simuliidae of the Culicomorpha infraorder.
Also known as warble flies or gadflies, the larvae of which insect family live as internal parasites in mammal flesh or gut, with one species routinely infesting humans?
Botfly: Parasitic insect. Dermatobia hominis is the only species of botfly known to parasitize humans routinely, though other species of flies cause myiasis in humans.
He piloted the Lunar Module Eagle in 1969 to become the second person to walk on the Moon, and after Jim Lovell's death in 2025 became the oldest living astronaut — who is he?
These biomolecules often follow the tidy empirical formula (CH2O)n, and as polysaccharides like starch, glycogen, and cellulose they store energy and build structure — what family are they?
Carbohydrate: Organic compound that consists only of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
Consisting mainly of the brain and spinal cord — and, surprisingly, the retina too — this part of the body integrates information to coordinate an animal's activity — what is it?
Central nervous system: Brain and spinal cord. The rest of this article exclusively discusses the vertebrate central nervous system, which is radically distinct from all other animals.
Patented in 1948, this first-generation antihistamine blocks the H1 receptor to relieve allergy symptoms like hay fever within about two hours — what is it?
Chlorphenamine: Antihistamine used to treat allergies.
First described by Linnaeus in 1758 and introduced to North America to control aphids, this red beetle with seven black spots gets its genus name from the Latin word for 'scarlet' — which species?
Coccinella septempunctata: Species of beetle. It inhabits many regions with a temperate climate.
The first bomber capable of Mach 2 flight, this 1950s delta-winged bomber carried its nuclear payload in a combination bomb-and-fuel pod slung beneath the fuselage — which bomber?
Convair B-58 Hustler: Cold War-era American supersonic bomber.
Caused by prolonged exposure to excess cortisol, this condition produces abdominal weight gain with thin limbs, a rounded red face, and reddish stretch marks — which condition is it?
Cushing's syndrome: Symptoms from excessive exposure to glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

Known mainly through DNA evidence rather than plentiful fossils, this extinct archaic human group ranged across Asia until about 32,000 years ago, and DNA analysis confirmed the Harbin skull belonged to it — what group is it?
Denisovan: Archaic human species from Asia.
Synthesized from L-DOPA in the brain and kidneys, this catecholamine acts as a neurotransmitter and drives a major brain pathway tied to reward and motivation — what is it?
Dopamine: Organic chemical that functions both as a hormone and a neurotransmitter.
This group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders causes loose joints and stretchy, velvety skin, with a classification last updated in 2017 — what condition is it?
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Group of genetic connective tissues disorders. The existing classification was last updated in 2017, when a number of rarer forms of EDS were added.
Despite never earning a university degree, this German-American psychoanalyst taught at Harvard, Berkeley, and Yale, and coined the term 'identity crisis' — who is he?
Erik Erikson: American psychoanalyst and essayist (1902–1994)

With a red face, a black-and-white head, and a bold yellow wing bar, this small finch native to the Palearctic often appears in Italian Renaissance paintings of the Madonna and Child. What bird is it?
European goldfinch: Species of bird. It has been introduced to other areas, including Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay and the United States.
Also called slapped cheek syndrome, this common childhood illness is caused by parvovirus B19, discovered in 1975 — what condition is it?
Fifth disease: Red rash due to infection with parvovirus B19.
This British-American theoretical physicist lent his name to a hypothetical genetically engineered 'tree' and a transform used in additive number theory — who was he?
Freeman Dyson: British theoretical physicist and mathematician (1923–2020)

Arriving late to a lecture, this mathematician copied down two famous unsolved problems in statistics, mistook them for homework — and solved them; he's better known for inventing the simplex algorithm for linear programming. Who was he?
Known online by the alias 'anakata,' this Swedish computer specialist co-founded a notorious BitTorrent site and later helped WikiLeaks with its 2010 release of a leaked military video — who is he?
Gottfrid Svartholm: Swedish computer specialist. Parts of an interview with Svartholm commenting on the May 2006 police raid of The Pirate Bay are featured in Good Copy Bad Copy and Steal This Film.

Derived independently in the 1830s by two European researchers and later given theoretical backing by George Stokes, this law describes the pressure drop of laminar flow through a drinking straw or a hypodermic needle — what's it called?
Hagen–Poiseuille equation: Law describing the pressure drop in an incompressible and Newtonian fluid.
Nicknamed for its shaggy white spines that dangle over a centimeter long, this edible mushroom is commonly called lion's mane and is used in traditional Chinese medicine — which fungus?
Hericium erinaceus: Edible mushroom. Hericium erinaceus, commonly known as lion's mane, yamabushitake, bearded tooth fungus, or bearded hedgehog, is a species of tooth fungus.
This climbing, hemp-family plant's female cone-shaped flowers are used to flavor and preserve beer — what's the scientific name for hops?
Humulus lupulus: Species of flowering plant.
Formed by the merger of two hip flexor muscles that join at the femur's lesser trochanter, this is the body's strongest flexor of the hip — what is it called?
Iliopsoas: Joined psoas and iliacus muscles of the hip and thigh.
A self-taught rocketeer and practicing occultist, this co-founder of both JPL and Aerojet invented the first castable composite rocket propellant before dying young in 1952. Who was he?
This English mathematician dreamed up the cellular automaton known as the Game of Life and spent his later years at Princeton — who was he?
This German-Finnish internet entrepreneur founded the file-hosting service Megaupload before U.S. authorities seized it in 2012 — who is he?
This biennial vegetable in the onion family has an edible bundle of leaf sheaths sometimes colloquially called a 'stem' — what is it?
Leek: Vegetable in the onion family. A leek is a biennial vegetable, a cultivar of Allium ampeloprasum, the broadleaf wild leek (syn.
Named after both a biblical sea monster and the author of 'Moby-Dick,' this extinct predatory sperm whale roamed ancient oceans roughly 9 million years ago — which genus?
Livyatan: Extinct genus of sperm whale from the Miocene epoch.
Marketed by Apple since 2001 for its line of Mac computers, this proprietary operating system derives from OPENSTEP for Mach and FreeBSD. What kind of system is it?
macOS, previously OS X and originally Mac OS X, is a proprietary Unix operating system derived from OPENSTEP for Mach and FreeBSD, marketed and developed by Apple since 2001.
The heaviest members of the squirrel family, these ground-dwelling herbivores live in groups through the summer before disappearing underground to hibernate all winter — what are they?
Marmot: Genus of mammals (large ground squirrels)
This rose-family shrub, commonly known as the medlar, produces fruit that's traditionally eaten only after it has softened past ripeness — what's its scientific name?
Mespilus germanica: Fruit tree, the medlar. Mespilus germanica, known as the medlar or common medlar, is a large shrub or small tree in the rose family Rosaceae.
Named for the Latin for 'thousand feet,' no species of this many-legged arthropod class was confirmed to have 1,000-plus legs until a 2020 discovery with over 1,300 — what are they?
Millipede: Class of arthropods. Its primary defence mechanism is to curl into a tight coil, thereby protecting its legs and other vital delicate areas on the body behind a hard exoskeleton.
Grown above the upper lip and below the nose, this facial hair style has taken many forms across history — what is it called?
Moustache: Strip of facial hair across the upper lip. A moustache (UK:) or mustache (US:) is a growth of facial hair grown above the upper lip and under the nose of men.

Attributed to 19th-century pathologist Rudolf Virchow, this term for the premature death of cells caused by trauma or infection contrasts with the body's own programmed cell death — what's the condition called?
Necrosis: Unprogrammed cell death caused by external cell injury.
Introduced to Hawaii in 1929, this crested songbird serves as the state bird of seven US states including Ohio and Virginia — which bird?
Northern cardinal: Species of North American bird.
A woody perennial native to the Mediterranean and a close relative of sweet marjoram, this mint-family herb is a staple of Italian and Greek cooking — what is it?
This skin sensation includes the classic 'pins and needles' feeling when a limb falls asleep, and can also be triggered by hitting your funny bone — what is it called?
Paresthesia: Dermal sensation with no physical cause.

Caused by a lack of intrinsic factor — often from an autoimmune attack on the stomach — this vitamin B12 deficiency disorder brings gradual fatigue, a smooth red tongue, and numbness in the hands and feet — which condition?
Pernicious anemia: Lack of red blood cells due to vitamin B12 deficiency.
Evergreen conifers of the genus Pinus, these trees grow their needle leaves in bunches of two to five and yield both the nuts used in pesto and the resin that flavors retsina wine?
Pine: Genus of coniferous trees. A pine is any conifer in the genus Pinus of the family Pinaceae.
Better known in the kitchen as cream of tartar, this winemaking byproduct helps stabilize egg whites for fluffier meringues — what compound is it?
Potassium bitartrate: Chemical salt used in cooking as cream of tartar.
Crossing the line between the natural and social sciences, this discipline scientifically studies the mind and behavior — both conscious and unconscious — in humans and other animals. What is it?
Psychology: Study of mental functions and behaviors.
Also marketed as canola once bred to lower its naturally high erucic acid content, this yellow-flowered Brassicaceae crop is the world's third-largest source of vegetable oil — which plant?
Rapeseed: Plant species grown for its oil-rich seed.
Usually caused by a vitamin-D deficiency, this childhood condition softens bones and can produce bowed legs and stunted growth — the adult analogue is osteomalacia; what is it?
Sold under the brand name Ventolin, this fast-acting inhaled medication opens the airways within about 15 minutes to treat asthma attacks and COPD — what is it?
Salbutamol: Short-acting bronchodilator used for acute asthma.
Co-founder of the file-sharing service Napster, this entrepreneur became Facebook's first president before later founding a philanthropic foundation focused on life sciences — who is he?
Sean Parker: American entrepreneur and philanthropist (born 1979)

This Irish mathematician and physicist held Cambridge's Lucasian Professorship for an unmatched 54 years, leaving his name on equations of fluid mechanics and a theorem of vector calculus — who is it?
Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet: British mathematician and physicist (1819–1903)
This family of roughly 1,450 moths flies so swiftly on narrow wings and streamlined bodies that some species hover at flowers and are routinely mistaken for hummingbirds — what's its scientific name?
Sphingidae: Family of insects. The Sphingidae are a family of moths commonly called sphinx moths, also colloquially known as hawk moths, with many of their caterpillars known as hornworms.

Distinct from addiction, this biopsychological condition occurs when a person's body has adapted so much to a psychoactive drug that stopping triggers withdrawal, requiring continued use just to function — what is this condition called?
Substance dependence: Need for a drug, whose discontinuation results in withdrawal symptoms.
One of the largest parasitoid wasps, this creature paralyzes its eight-legged prey with a sting, drags it into a nest, and lays a single egg so the larva can devour the still-living host. What is it?
Tarantula hawk: Common name for two genera of wasps.
Best known for his 1651 work 'Leviathan' and its influential take on social contract theory, this English philosopher once met Galileo while tutoring the Cavendish family across Europe — who was he?
Thomas Hobbes: English philosopher and political theorist (1588–1679)
Only about 76 to 90 nucleotides long, this adaptor molecule reads each three-letter mRNA codon with a matching anticodon and ferries the right amino acid to the ribosome — what is it?
Transfer RNA: RNA that facilitates the addition of amino acids to a new protein.
Element 121, this not-yet-synthesized superactinide is expected to open a brand-new g-block of the periodic table and may sit on the 'island of stability' — what's its placeholder name?
Unbiunium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 121 (Ubu)
Named by a naturalist in 1821, this family of feliform mammals split into genets, civets, and palm civets, and spans Africa to Southeast Asia — what is it?
Viverridae: Family of carnivorans. Viverridae is a family of small to medium-sized feliform mammals, comprising 14 genera with 33 species.
Nominated by Einstein, this Austrian physicist won the 1945 Nobel Prize for describing the exclusion principle and, in 1930, proposed the tiny neutral particle later named the neutrino — who is he?
The symbol for niobium is Nb. Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb and atomic number 41.
The symbol for holmium is Ho. Holmium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ho and atomic number 67.
